pool.prompt: A carrier is upgrading an 80 km G.652 fiber route from 10 Gb/s to 100 Gb/s DWDM. Which characterization tests are most important before activation?
choices: Only OTDR testing at 1310 nm — the route is already G.652
CD characterization (to calculate dispersion compensation module requirements) and PMD measurement (to verify the route is within 100G coherent system tolerances)
Attenuation cut-back test on all fiber reels — no field tests needed
Connector end-face inspection only — 100G is self-correcting for dispersion
pool.explanation: For a DWDM upgrade, the critical parameters are CD profile (to size dispersion compensation) and PMD (to confirm the fiber is within the 100G coherent system's tolerance). A standard OTDR trace won't reveal CD or PMD — those require dedicated characterization instruments.

pool.prompt: An OTDR trace shows a 'gainer' event at a splice — the splice appears to have -0.2 dB loss (power increased after the splice). What should the technician do?
choices: Accept the result — the splice is working perfectly and adding signal
Replace the splice immediately — negative loss indicates a bad physical connection
Run a bidirectional OTDR test and average the two measurements — the apparent gain is a backscatter artifact caused by differing fiber backscatter coefficients, not real optical gain
Re-run the OTDR with a shorter pulse width to eliminate the artifact
pool.explanation: Gainers are OTDR backscatter artifacts when two fibers with different backscatter coefficients are spliced. The bidirectional average is the true splice loss — e.g., if one direction shows -0.2 dB and the other +0.4 dB, the true loss is (-0.2+0.4)/2 = 0.1 dB.
pool.citation: IEC 61280-4-2 (bidirectional OTDR testing for installed single-mode cable plant).

pool.prompt: What field method for chromatic dispersion (CD) measurement uses a modulated broadband source and measures the phase difference between wavelengths?
choices: The pulse-delay method
The phase-shift method
The cut-back method
The mandrel wrap method
pool.explanation: The phase-shift method injects a sinusoidally modulated broadband optical signal and measures the relative phase of the detected signal at different wavelengths. The phase difference is proportional to the group-delay difference, from which the dispersion coefficient D is calculated.

pool.prompt: Why is bidirectional OTDR testing standard practice for splice loss records, rather than accepting a single-direction measurement?
choices: Bidirectional testing is only needed for multimode fiber

Single-direction OTDR measurements can show a splice as artificially better OR worse than its true loss due to backscatter-coefficient mismatch between the two spliced fibers; averaging both directions cancels out that artifact
Bidirectional testing is faster than single-direction testing
Single-direction testing cannot detect any splice events at all
pool.explanation: Backscatter coefficient differences between two spliced fibers bias a single-direction OTDR reading — sometimes showing a 'gainer' (apparent negative loss), sometimes an inflated loss. Averaging measurements from both directions cancels this artifact and yields the true splice loss.
pool.citation: IEC 61280-4-2 — bidirectional attenuation/ORL measurement for installed single-mode cable plant.

choices: Fusion splicer calibration procedures
Attenuation and optical return loss (ORL) measurement of installed single-mode fiber optic cable plant, including bidirectional OTDR testing practices
Manufacturing tolerances for buffer tube color coding
RUS materials acceptance testing for buried conduit
pool.explanation: IEC 61280-4-2 covers attenuation and ORL measurement of installed single-mode cable plant (fibers, connectors, splices, and other passive devices) across residential, commercial, industrial, data center, and OSP environments, including OTDR configuration and bidirectional testing guidance.
pool.citation: IEC 61280-4-2, Fibre-optic communication subsystem test procedures — Part 4-2.

pool.prompt: Why can't a standard OTDR trace reveal a fiber route's PMD value?
choices: OTDR and PMD measurement are the same test with different names

A standard OTDR measures backscattered light intensity vs. distance (for loss/event location); PMD is a polarization-dependent timing effect that requires a dedicated PMD test instrument (e.g., interferometric or fixed-analyzer methods), not an OTDR
OTDR can measure PMD, but only above 1550 nm
PMD can only be measured in a laboratory, never in the field
pool.explanation: OTDR and PMD testing measure fundamentally different physical phenomena. OTDR characterizes loss and reflectance events along a fiber's length using backscattered light. PMD requires specialized instrumentation that measures polarization-dependent group delay, which an OTDR is not designed to detect.

pool.prompt: A splice gainer of -0.2 dB in one direction and +0.4 dB in the reverse direction are recorded for the same splice. What is the correct averaged splice loss value to record?
choices: -0.2 dB (accept the more favorable reading)
+0.4 dB (accept the more conservative reading)
0.1 dB (the average of the two directional readings)
0.6 dB (the sum of the two directional readings)
pool.explanation: Bidirectional averaging: (-0.2 + 0.4) / 2 = 0.1 dB. This cancels the backscatter-coefficient artifact and yields the splice's true loss, which is neither the artificially low nor artificially high single-direction reading.

pool.prompt: Before activating a 100G coherent DWDM system on an existing 80 km G.652 route originally built for 10 Gb/s, why is CD compensation module sizing dependent on field-measured CD, not just the fiber's ITU-T spec value?
choices: Field-measured CD is always identical to the spec value, so measurement is unnecessary

Real installed fiber's CD can vary from a single generic spec figure due to manufacturing variation, splicing of different fiber vintages/types along the route, and temperature — field characterization gives the actual value needed to correctly size compensation rather than relying on an assumed nominal figure
CD compensation modules are sized only by distance, never by measured dispersion
CD only matters for multimode fiber, not the SMF route described
pool.explanation: A real 80 km route may include fiber from multiple manufacturing runs, possibly even different fiber vintages spliced together over the years, each with slightly different actual CD. Field-measuring the actual accumulated CD (rather than assuming a textbook nominal value) is what lets an engineer correctly size the dispersion compensation module for that specific route.
